report:
I have strong consistent evidence from multiple systematic reviews/meta-analyses of RCTs. This is sufficient to write the report.

## Conclusion: Yes — offering HIV self-testing increases HIV testing uptake

The evidence strongly supports that **offering HIV self-testing (HIVST) causally increases the uptake and frequency of HIV testing**, compared with standard testing services alone.

**Key evidence:**

1. **General population meta-analysis** (Eshun-Wilson et al., *EClinicalMedicine*, 2021): Pooling 13 RCTs, HIVST **more than doubled** testing uptake (RR 2.09, 95% CI 1.69–2.58) with moderate-certainty GRADE evidence. Effects were seen "by nearly all" (12/13) trials individually. (https://www.thelancet.com/journals/eclinm/article/PIIS2589-5370(21)00271-6/fulltext)

2. **Key populations meta-analysis** (same research group, *BMC Medicine*, 2020): A systematic review of RCTs comparing HIVST to standard testing among key populations (sex workers, MSM, people who inject drugs) similarly found increased testing uptake and frequency across delivery models, informing new WHO recommendations. (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12916-020-01835-z)

3. **Umbrella review** (*PLOS ONE*, 2021), synthesizing prior systematic reviews, concluded HIVST "has the potential to increase the uptake of HIV testing compared to standard HIV testing services," with the strongest gains when HIVST is paired with optional home-based linkage to care, which also improved HIV positivity detection and linkage. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33503050/)

4. **Randomized trial in high-risk MSM** (Seattle) found HIVST increased testing frequency, though raised (unconfirmed) concerns about reduced counseling. (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6037557/)

**Assessment of evidence quality:** This conclusion rests on multiple RCTs, aggregated in two independent, high-quality meta-analyses/systematic reviews (moderate-certainty GRADE ratings), across both general and key populations, in varied settings (workplace, partner distribution, community). The consistency across trial designs and populations, plus WHO's incorporation of these findings into testing guidelines, gives high confidence that the effect is causal and robust, not merely correlational.
